title: Have scientists found the secret to eternal power?
gist: After a century of false starts, space-based solar power is nearing commercial viability thanks to cheaper reusable rockets and modular satellite designs like Space Solar's Cassiopeia, with the AI data-centre power crunch—not climate policy—now the strongest driver of investor and government interest, even as UK government funding has dried up and China races ahead with a state-backed roadmap.

insights.claim: UK startup Space Solar, co-founded by Martin Soltau and Sam Adlen, is developing a sun-pointing satellite over a kilometre wide weighing 800 tonnes that would sit in geosynchronous orbit roughly 36,000km above Earth and beam more than 600 megawatts of power to Earth via microwave, 24 hours a day.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Defines the scale of the flagship UK space-solar project (600MW+, comparable to a mid-size power station) that investors and policymakers are being asked to back.
insights.locator: Their ambition, shared with chief technical officer David Homfray

insights.claim: Space-based solar power avoids clouds, nightfall and seasons, receiving sunlight roughly 13 times more intense than a solar panel gets on a cloudy afternoon in Britain, giving it a fundamentally different capacity factor than terrestrial solar.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: The core physical advantage underpinning the entire investment thesis: near-100% capacity-factor solar power that could help grids handle the intermittency problem plaguing terrestrial renewables.
insights.locator: In space there are no clouds, no nightfall, no seasons

insights.claim: In January 1973, Czech-American engineer Peter Glaser, who had worked on solar power for Apollo 11, was granted a US patent for a two-satellite geosynchronous solar power design, arguing the US needed alternatives to finite oil and gas—but was skeptical of both nuclear fission (expensive, hazardous, toxic waste) and nuclear fusion, which he called 'a physicist's impossible dream.'
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Establishes space-solar as a decades-old engineering concept with an early, prescient critic of fusion economics whose skepticism the article's modern sources still echo.
insights.locator: Glaser, who had worked on solar power in the Apollo 11 moon programme

insights.claim: US federal interest in space solar collapsed after a 1979 NASA/Department of Energy study found a 300-gigawatt system built from 60 satellites was technically achievable, but the government scrapped the project over cost uncertainty and environmental concerns, despite $20m in prior research funding.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Shows the technology has previously been deemed technically feasible at gigawatt scale but killed on cost/political grounds—useful base rate for assessing whether today's renewed enthusiasm will suffer the same fate.
insights.locator: the government scrapped the project over uncertain costs

insights.claim: In 2013, property billionaire Donald Bren secretly donated $100m to Caltech to fund a space-based solar demonstration mission; the resulting Space Solar Power Demonstrator launched in January 2023 and successfully beamed power from space to Earth for the first time, completing its mission in November 2023.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: The first-ever successful space-to-Earth power beaming demonstration is the proof point re-energizing the entire sector; private philanthropy, not government funding, delivered it.
insights.locator: Launched in January 2023, the Space Solar Power Demonstrator

insights.claim: Space Solar's chief architect Ian Cash filed core patents in 2017-2018 for a design called Cassiopeia, which uses large fixed mirrors and steers its power beam electronically across 360 degrees with no moving parts, is lighter and cheaper than earlier mechanical designs, can be assembled in orbit from hundreds of mass-produced identical modules, and remains functional even if part of it is damaged.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: The core engineering breakthrough underlying Space Solar's commercial pitch: modular, damage-resistant, mass-manufacturable satellite design solves the cost and fragility problems that killed earlier space-solar proposals.
insights.locator: In 2017 and 2018, he filed the core patents

insights.claim: NASA veteran John Mankins, who spent 25 years on space solar power, developed a competing modular design called SPS-Alpha inspired by how bee hives and ant colonies build structures from many small identical units; a 2012 NASA-funded study he led estimated such a system could eventually deliver electricity at around 9 cents per kilowatt-hour, competitive with or cheaper than conventional sources.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: An independent, NASA-backed cost estimate (9 cents/kWh) supports the commercial viability case for modular space-solar architectures beyond just Space Solar's own claims.
insights.quote: If we’d pursued space solar power in the 1980s, the platforms would be operational today.
insights.locator: A Nasa-funded study that Mankins led in 2012

themes.theme: UK policy: a funding gap despite a favourable feasibility study

insights.claim: A 2020 UK government-commissioned Frazer-Nash report, led by Martin Soltau, concluded space-based solar power was technically feasible, competitively priced against other clean energy sources, and would deliver substantial manufacturing and jobs benefits, proposing a 'first of a kind' 2GW satellite (equivalent to a nuclear power station's output) whose receiving antennas would need only a third of the land area of an equivalent terrestrial solar farm.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: An official UK government-commissioned study already validated the technical and economic case for space solar at gigawatt scale—the policy question is funding follow-through, not feasibility.
insights.locator: The resulting report, which was led by Soltau

insights.claim: The 2020 UK Frazer-Nash report proposed a staged roadmap: demonstrate the technology in space by 2031, deliver a first operational grid-feeding system by 2040, and reach roughly 15 per cent of UK electricity demand from space-based solar by the early 2040s, at an estimated total cost of £16-17bn, with public funding of about £350m over five years for the first phase before private capital would take over.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated UK deployment roadmap and cost/funding split (£350m public seed capital against a £16-17bn total) that gives investors a benchmark timeline and capital structure to track against actual funding delivered.
insights.locator: It suggested that a staged development programme

insights.claim: Following the 2020 report, the UK launched a £6m feasibility study in 2022 split between BEIS and the UK Space Agency, but dedicated government funding for space-based solar power has since dried up after energy policy was moved to the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero, which deprioritized the initiative in favour of other technologies.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
entities: Department of Energy Security and Net Zero
insights.so_what: Documents a specific UK government funding reversal/deprioritization event—key context for assessing political and financing risk to the UK space-solar sector versus rival national programmes.
insights.quote: BEIS saw space solar power as a way of decarbonising the grid: it was an energy problem. When energy [department] pulled out, the space people saw no reason to continue.
insights.locator: As one industry insider close to the programme explained

insights.claim: Space Solar co-CEO Martin Soltau contrasts UK government funding of £400m (initial) plus a further £1.3bn for a prototype fusion power plant in Nottinghamshire, plus £45m for a fusion-dedicated AI supercomputer, against near-zero ongoing funding for space-based solar, arguing fusion's 'holy grail' promise of cheap infinite energy is unlikely to be delivered because there is still no costed design for a commercial fusion reactor.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A direct, quantified critique of UK energy R&D capital allocation—over £1.7bn committed to fusion versus a dried-up space-solar programme—relevant to investors weighing UK clean-energy technology bets against government funding signals.
insights.quote: We have an engineered design. They do not.
insights.locator: His frustration, shared with other supporters of space-based solar

insights.claim: David Homfrey, Space Solar's colleague and formerly the engineer in charge of the Joint European Torus (the world's largest fusion experiment) who led a £220m programme to commercialize fusion power, concluded that fusion commercialization was unlikely to work.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: An insider fusion-programme leader turning skeptic on fusion and pivoting to space solar is a high-signal credibility marker for investors deciding between competing next-generation clean-power technology bets.
insights.locator: David Homfrey, now Soltau’s colleague at Space Solar

insights.claim: Space Solar co-CEO Martin Soltau warns that Britain currently leads on space-based solar power technology but 'we won't be for long,' framing continued underfunding as a first-mover advantage the UK risks squandering to international competitors.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A time-limited competitive-advantage claim that frames UK funding decisions in the next few years as decisive for whether the country captures the economic upside of a technology it currently leads.
insights.quote: We are in the lead now, but we won’t be for long.
insights.locator: Soltau argues that Britain is in a strong position

themes.theme: The global race: China, Japan, ESA and the US

insights.claim: China has pursued space-based solar power at national scale since 2013, after two senior academics wrote to Xi Jinping urging investment; the China Academy for Space Technology has since demonstrated earthbound beaming to multiple targets, a national committee on space solar power was established in 2021, and the country's Omega system aims to supply 2GW of power to Earth by 2050, with space solar power now included in China's latest five-year plan.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: China has built a decade-long, state-backed roadmap with demonstrated technical progress (multi-target beaming) and an explicit 2050 gigawatt-scale target now embedded in national planning—the most credible sovereign competitor to Western space-solar efforts.
insights.locator: China, meanwhile, has approached the technology with characteristic scale

insights.claim: Japan's government called in 2009 for the country to 'lead the world in space-based solar power' with a full-scale system targeted for 2030, but that ambition has since slipped, while the European Space Agency's Solaris initiative assessed gigawatt-scale orbital power stations but failed to garner enough enthusiasm among member states to move into practice.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Both Japan and the EU have stalled on space-solar commitments despite early ambition, leaving China and now a UK/US private-sector push as the more active fronts—relevant for gauging where public capital is actually flowing.
insights.locator: In 2009, the Japanese government called for a programme

insights.claim: There is growing military interest in space-based solar power from both China and the US because it could replace vulnerable diesel-generator supply convoys at remote military bases, where fuel delivery costs in war zones can run into hundreds of dollars per gallon before counting the cost of lives lost defending convoys.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Identifies defence procurement as a near-term, high-willingness-to-pay customer segment for space-solar technology, independent of civilian grid economics—a potential earlier revenue path for developers.
insights.locator: There’s a keen military interest from countries including China and the US

insights.claim: China's ambitions for a permanent lunar base, water-ice mining at the lunar south pole, and eventual asteroid mining will require far more power than conventional solar arrays can supply, positioning orbiting power-beaming satellites as potential infrastructure for lunar and space-based manufacturing as well as Earth power.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Extends the space-solar addressable market beyond Earth-based electricity to off-world infrastructure, a long-horizon but potentially large adjacent market tied to the broader lunar/asteroid resource race.
insights.locator: China’s ambitions for a permanent lunar base

themes.theme: AI power demand as the new catalyst

insights.claim: Elon Musk once called space-based solar power 'one of the stupidest ideas' he had ever heard, but has since become 'a fervent advocate,' a shift the article attributes to the AI-driven data-centre power crunch that has changed the economics of terrestrial versus orbital power generation.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A high-profile skeptic-to-advocate conversion driven by AI power scarcity is a strong signal that the investment case for space solar has shifted from a climate play to an AI infrastructure play.
insights.locator: The world’s first trillionaire, Musk once called space-based solar

insights.claim: Global electricity demand from AI data centres is projected to double in five years, reaching 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, while the 'Big Five' hyperscalers—Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle—are expected to spend approximately $725bn on AI infrastructure in 2026 alone, a 77 per cent increase on 2025 and more than the entire GDP of Switzerland.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the AI infrastructure capex wave ($725bn in 2026, +77% YoY) that is now the primary demand driver being cited to justify space-based solar investment, a key macro data point for AI infrastructure and power-sector investors.
insights.locator: The Big Five hyperscalers

insights.claim: Despite huge capital outlays, the US electricity market already has a 9.3GW shortfall in capacity for AI data centres, which Goldman Sachs projects could widen to 45GW by 2028, with hyperscalers facing shortages of critical minerals, long grid-connection waiting lists and gas-turbine delays severe enough that some are contemplating a return to coal.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourced power-shortfall forecast (9.3GW now, up to 45GW by 2028) that quantifies the scale of the US AI power bottleneck—directly relevant to power-sector, utility and AI-infrastructure investment theses.
insights.locator: the US market now has 9.3GW shortfall in capacity

insights.claim: Elon Musk's company resorted to using dozens of unregulated natural gas turbines to power supercomputer clusters in Memphis, Tennessee, illustrating how severe grid-connection and power-supply constraints have become for AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A concrete real-world example of an AI hyperscaler bypassing normal grid/regulatory power procurement due to acute shortages—illustrates near-term power scarcity risk to AI datacentre buildout timelines.
insights.locator: Musk’s firm resorted to using dozens of unregulated natural gas turbines

themes.theme: Economics, commercial applications and cost trajectory

insights.claim: Space Solar co-CEO Martin Soltau estimates the levelised cost of space-based solar power could be around £30 per megawatt-hour at current prices—below the £100+/MWh cost of intermittent UK wind power—and could fall to as little as £10/MWh if launch costs decline further, though he cautions that 'if SpaceX have a monopoly, the prices may stay high.'
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified cost claim (£30/MWh, falling to £10/MWh) that positions space solar as potentially cheaper than UK wind power, while flagging launch-provider concentration (SpaceX) as a key cost and pricing-power risk to the whole sector.
insights.quote: if the prices remain broadly the same as today, our levelised cost is £30 a megawatt hour
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Soltau estimates

insights.claim: A satellite in low-Earth orbit or geostationary orbit can beam power to a wide geographic footprint—for example, one satellite over Nairobi could sell electricity to the UK, India, Tashkent, the Middle East or across Africa, while another positioned further west could reach Brazil or the US east coast—enabling a supplier to sell to the highest bidder across roughly a third of the planet at any given moment, 24/7.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Describes a novel commercial model unique to orbital power generation—real-time, cross-border electricity arbitrage to the highest global bidder—a structurally different revenue model than any terrestrial power asset.
insights.locator: According to Mark Garnier, a Conservative MP

insights.claim: Mark Garnier, a Conservative MP and non-executive director of Space Solar who holds share options in the company, no longer lobbies government on the project's behalf because of that financial interest, illustrating both the commercial promotion around the technology and a related governance/conflict-of-interest consideration.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A disclosed conflict-of-interest detail relevant to assessing the credibility and independence of commercial claims being made about Space Solar's prospects by figures with equity in the company.
insights.locator: who no longer lobbies government on behalf of the project

insights.claim: Space Solar is piloting a project with the British Antarctic Survey to beam power from low-Earth orbit to British scientists in Antarctica, addressing the Survey's inability to decarbonise its own remote operations despite its climate-science mission.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Identifies remote/off-grid scientific and disaster-relief operations as an early, near-term commercial use case for space-solar power ahead of full grid-scale deployment.
insights.locator: We’re working very closely with the British Antarctic Survey

insights.claim: A NASA lifecycle assessment published in January 2024 concluded that current space-based solar designs remain between 12 and 80 times more expensive than terrestrial renewables, though Space Solar advocates argue those figures are now out of date.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A credible, dated official cost estimate that directly contradicts industry claims of near-term cost competitiveness—an important counterweight investors should track against future updated assessments.
insights.locator: A Nasa lifecycle assessment published in January 2024

insights.claim: Because satellites in geostationary orbit do not naturally burn up on re-entry the way low-orbit satellites do, large-scale deployment of space-based solar power would meaningfully add to long-term space debris risk unless careful recovery plans are developed; astronomers also fear vast reflective orbital structures would degrade dark and quiet skies.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Identifies two under-addressed externalities—space debris and astronomical light pollution—that could invite future regulatory pushback or added compliance costs on the sector.
insights.locator: Some astronomers fear that vast reflective structures

insights.claim: Securing radio spectrum allocation for space-based solar power through the UN's International Telecommunication Union and national regulators like Ofcom is a slow, multilateral process that could add decades of delay to deployment, on top of unproven robotics for in-orbit construction and unknown structural stresses on kilometre-scale satellites in geostationary orbit.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Regulatory and technical-readiness risk—not just financing—could be the binding constraint on deployment timelines; investors should track ITU/Ofcom spectrum processes as a leading indicator of real-world progress.
insights.locator: Securing the radio spectrum allocations demanded

insights.claim: Henri Barde, a retired former head of space power systems at the European Space Agency, is skeptical that systems of this scale and complexity can be deployed within a meaningful timeframe, noting that investors and governments have balked at the huge, unguaranteed investment required, and calls space-based solar power 'a beautiful idea that may never happen.'
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A credentialed former ESA insider provides the article's strongest counter-thesis, arguing the technology risk and capital-risk profile may permanently deter the large-scale investment needed—an important bear case to weigh against the bullish industry claims.
insights.quote: a beautiful idea that may never happen
insights.locator: Space-based solar power, in his view

insights.claim: Martin Soltau believes space-based solar power could be commercialized within five to six years if the project moved at the pace of the private sector rather than government, arguing that without sufficient will and ambition, 'anything is decades away.'
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Sets an aggressive 5-6 year commercialization timeline explicitly conditional on private-sector-speed execution—a benchmark to track Space Solar's actual progress against as a gauge of whether the bullish case is playing out.
insights.quote: If we don’t have the will, anything is decades away.
insights.locator: In his view, space-based solar could be commercialised
